## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)

*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*

The *Cūḷapalobhanajātaka* (Ja 263), translated in modern cataloging as *The Shorter Tale of Allure*, is a canonical birth-story preserved in the Jātaka collection of the Khuddaka Nikāya [SuttaCentral]. Set at Jetavana, the story's frame narrative concerns a backsliding monk whom the Buddha summons to the Hall of Truth [SuttaCentral]. Upon confirming that the monk is faltering in his practice, the Buddha remarks that in past times women caused even believing souls to fall into wrongdoing, whereupon he recounts the story of the past [SuttaCentral]. In modern studies, Julius Evola quotes a verse from this Jātaka ("seducers and astute, they destroy the noble life") in his analysis of ascetic detachment and monastic attitudes toward sensual allure [Evola 1995].

No cross-language parallels in Sanskrit, Chinese, or Tibetan are identified for this discourse on SuttaCentral or DharmaNexus [SuttaCentral; DharmaNexus]. However, computational text-reuse analysis shows significant internal Pali matches [DharmaNexus]. In particular, verses or text segments (§1.1–3.4) are shared with its longer companion narrative, the *Mahāpalobhanajātaka* (Ja 507, §24.4–28.4), as well as the *Kuṇālajātaka* (Ja 536, where §2.1–3.4 closely aligns with §100.3–102.4) [DharmaNexus]. Portions of this text are likewise repeated within two volumes of the *Jātaka-aṭṭhakathā* (Dutiyo bhāgo and Catuttho bhāgo) [DharmaNexus]. SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages [SuttaCentral].
